a: Fraudulent messages that trick people into disclosing personal information by pretending to be trustworthy
Software that encrypts your files
Flooding a server with traffic
Entering code into a text box
tasks.fb: This is the exam definition: an online fraud technique that disguises itself as a trustworthy institution.

tasks.q: Why is phishing called social engineering?
a: It manipulates people rather than attacking the technology
It only works on social media
It engineers new software
It needs a social club
tasks.fb: Social engineering exploits trust, fear and habit.

tasks.q: What is the main aim of a phishing attack?
a: To get the victim to hand over information such as passwords or bank details
To slow down the victim's computer
To test the victim's antivirus
To improve the victim's spam filter
tasks.fb: It's fraud: the victim gives the information away.

tasks.q: Why do attackers target staff logins at a company?
a: One stolen login can give access to the whole network
Staff computers are faster
Staff emails are more fun to read
It makes the attacker an employee
tasks.fb: Many big breaches start with one phished password.

tasks.q: Which of these are warning signs of phishing? Select all that apply.
opts: The sender's address doesn't match the organisation
The message threatens that your account will close today
A generic greeting such as 'Dear customer'
A link that goes to an unfamiliar web address
The email is from someone in your contacts you emailed yesterday
The company's real logo is used
correct: The sender's address doesn't match the organisation
The message threatens that your account will close today
A generic greeting such as 'Dear customer'
A link that goes to an unfamiliar web address
tasks.fb: Attackers copy real logos easily, so a good-looking logo proves nothing.

tasks.q: Which address is most likely to be genuine for a bank called Bank?
a: www.bank.co.uk
www.bank.co.uk.login.ru
www.bank-secure-login.com
www.bank.verify-account.net
tasks.fb: Read the address from the right: the part just before the first single slash is the real domain.

tasks.q: Does a padlock in the address bar mean a site is safe?
a: No: it only means the connection is encrypted
Yes, always
Yes, if the site has a logo
Only on phones
tasks.fb: Criminals can get certificates for their fake sites too.

a: A phishing message aimed at one person, using personal details to look convincing
Phishing sent to millions of people
Phishing by post
Phishing that uses malware only
tasks.fb: Attackers gather details from social media to make it believable.

tasks.q: A text message says a parcel is held and asks you to pay a fee. What is this?
a: Smishing
Whaling
A worm
A denial-of-service attack

tasks.q: You get an email asking you to confirm your password. What should you do?
a: Don't click. Check with the organisation using contact details you already trust
Reply with the password to check if it's real
Forward it to your friends
Click the link but type carefully
tasks.fb: No genuine organisation asks for your password by email.

tasks.q: You clicked a phishing link and typed your password. What's the first thing to do?
a: Change that password immediately, and any account that shares it
Wait and see if anything happens
Turn the computer off for a week
Delete the email and say nothing
tasks.fb: Speed limits the damage, and telling the IT team helps protect everyone else.

tasks.q: Is each feature a phishing warning sign, or normal for a genuine message?
items: 'Dear customer, your account will be closed in 24 hours'
A link that goes to bank.co.uk.secure-login.ru
A receipt from a shop you used yesterday, with your name on it
A newsletter you signed up for, with an unsubscribe link
A message asking you to reply with your password
A school email from a teacher's usual address about homework
tasks.fb: Remember: urgency, odd addresses and requests for details are the big three.

info.title: Where the name comes from
info.text: 'Phishing' is a play on 'fishing': attackers cast out bait and wait to see who bites. The 'ph' comes from 'phreaking', an old form of phone hacking.

info.title: Millions a day
info.text: Billions of phishing emails are sent every day. Even a success rate far below 1% makes it worth the attackers' time.

info.title: Report it
info.text: In the UK, suspicious emails can be forwarded to report@phishing.gov.uk, and suspicious texts to 7726.

info.title: Clever fakes
info.text: Attackers register domains that look almost identical to real ones, sometimes using letters from other alphabets that look the same.

info.title: Two-factor helps
info.text: Even if a password is phished, a second factor, such as a code on your phone, usually stops the attacker getting in.

info.title: Simulated phishing
info.text: Many organisations send their own fake phishing emails to staff as training, then offer extra help to anyone who clicks.
